Poshan Haiming owns the retained deployment, letting his mouth flap once each year — all the sweet melons and the bitter melons told out together, while the crowd that cannot offer them gets the comet-star and sand in the eye.

Senses.Explanation: The once-each-year of the Chan records: the ritual calendar's single yearly round — counted at the solstice, handed as incense, laughed over the tea, and priced as an annual disaster by turns. Zhufeng Zhenxu raises the whisk and rules Old Gautama's day a once-each-year disaster for his descendants, while he, the seat-follower Xu, rises and falls along with him, each at his own convenience, before the donor feast where pearl and jade are all flung away and the Vulture-peak assembly seems never to have dispersed, Yezhu Fuhui, wild monk of the mountain, after the meal strongly brewing the East Court tea, sends word to the way-attainers everywhere — once each year laughing at cloud-mists — and asked what the laugh is, holds a long silence: the wall bursts, the lamp flies at the trees, the rafter slips, the moon leaks through the robe, Lianfeng Su counts one heat each year and one cold each year at the solstice — the massed yin stripped away, one yang reborn, great houses and village elders congratulating each other while the man of the groves sees only leaf-fall at the treetops and frost heaped at the roof-corner, dozing hooded in his patched blanket, and Shanyi Ruchun, at the founder's memorial, weighs the hundred-thousand-li sea crossing, the loss at the emperor's court, the uprooting before the peak, the tricked arm-cutting that killed the heroic spirits' laughter for a thousand years — why then once each year one burning of incense, the five tones and six pitches each finding their key? Shaweng Huihai on his own annual day is ashamed the way-work lies fallow while once each year he draws the crowd busy — mounting the hall, standing in for the drum, saying nothing, borrowing tortoise-hair to spread it, until seeing and hearing open wide in a laughing face, Zizhou Chuan, reciting the seventeenth generation's Ying'an Hua at the grand memorial, concedes the old teacher's whole career — every trick failing to close, twenty years on the curving chair, sheep's heads hung and dog meat sold — proof-less, and yet the incense burns once each year while a thousand years' regret cuts deeper, Feiyin Tongrong at the old teacher's memorial day asks what the season is — the deedless body shown, the stilling teaching spoken, neither eye-seen nor ear-heard — and answers: the once-each-year incense day, the whole realm manifest with nothing hidden, and Poshan Haiming on the enlightenment day lets his mouth flap once each year — all the sweet melons and the bitter melons told out together, while the crowd that cannot offer them gets the comet-star and sand in the eye.
